site.name: Buddha Dev Biswas
roles: teacher who helps law students to understand society
site.bio: I teach sociology at Karnataka State Law University, Hubballi, and I am a doctoral researcher at the Institute for Social and Economic Change, Bengaluru. I study how caste and identity are claimed, recognised and lived; how young people come to want the lives they want; and how publics decide whether a protest is legitimate.

research.intro: How categories of identity become consequential, and how people live with, use and contest them.

thesis.label: Doctoral research · ISEC, Bengaluru
thesis.title: Aspiration as Orientation: Youth and Their Futures Through and Beyond Educational and Occupational Pathways
thesis.text: Policy and research often read aspiration as a destination: a degree, a job, a rank. This study asks what that reading leaves out. It treats aspiration as an orientation toward a life a young person has reason to value, and follows how that orientation forms, how it relates to educational and occupational plans, and how social position shapes the ways it can be pursued.

in_progress.title: The Negotiated–Embodied Caste: Mobility, Recognition and the Asymmetric Marking of Caste in Contemporary India
in_progress.text: A framework for why caste persists: it is embedded in bodies, perception and bureaucratic identity, yet that embeddedness is continually negotiated through mobility and state recognition.

in_progress.title: The Two Archives
in_progress.text: How caste identity is held in two registers, the social and the documentary, and why documentary claims tend to move in one direction only. Draws on Kudmi-Mahato fieldwork.

in_progress.title: Public reasoning about the legitimacy of protest
in_progress.text: A qualitative study of how members of the public judged whether the 2026 NEET protest in India was legitimate, read through online discourse.

in_progress.title: Recognising the Other: a gateway mechanism of discrimination
in_progress.text: Why the same prejudiced person discriminates in one situation and not another. The paper argues that categorical identification of the other is a condition for prejudice to become practice, and plans classroom experiments to test it.
